subject: psychology
topic: Your most vivid memories are not your most accurate ones
angle: Flashbulb memories are characterized by high confidence and vividness rather than superior accuracy, as their consistency declines over time just like everyday memories.
title: The Illusion of Vivid Memory

hooks.text: Is your memory lying to you?
You trust your feelings over the facts.

reveal.headline: Vivid memories are not more accurate.
reveal.body: The clarity of a memory does not correlate with its factual consistency. Your most intense recollections are just as prone to decay as your mundane ones.

explain.headline: Confidence is a feeling, not a fact.
explain.body: Flashbulb memories feel more vivid and clear than everyday memories. However, their consistency declines over time at the same rate as ordinary memories.

matters.headline: Your feelings are not a record.
matters.body: That may be why you feel certain about your past even when you are wrong. The intensity of a moment can mask the erosion of the details.

example.headline: A kitchen at midnight.
example.body: You stand in the dark kitchen. You remember the exact light on the counter. You are certain of every detail. Time has likely altered most of them.

question.headline: What parts of your history are you sure of?

verdict: The evidence shows that while flashbulb memories feel more accurate and vivid than everyday memories, they do not actually maintain higher levels of consistency over time.
caveat: The studies often rely on self-reported ratings of confidence and vividness rather than objective measures of factual accuracy.
caption:
The most vivid memories are often the least reliable. 

Research shows that flashbulb memories feel more clear than everyday memories, but they do not stay consistent over time. These studies rely on self-reported confidence rather than objective accuracy.
